title: Expand Available Storage | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Expand Available Storage

HyperVault supports expanding an existing distributed cluster by adding a new server pool. Each pool expands the total available storage capacity of the cluster. HyperVault does not support increasing storage through logical volume expansion, rolling drive replacement, or other filesystem-level approaches.

Expansion does not provide Business Continuity/Disaster Recovery (BC/DR)-grade protections. While each pool is an independent set of servers with distinct erasure sets for availability, the complete loss of one pool results in HyperVault stopping I/O for all pools in the cluster. Similarly, an erasure set which loses quorum in one pool represents data loss of objects stored in that set, regardless of the number of other erasure sets or pools.

While HyperVault does not strictly require that the new server pool use the same type or size of hardware and software configuration as any existing server pool, HyperVault strongly recommends a similar configuration. This allows for simplified cluster management and more predictable performance across pools. For example, if your existing cluster has a pool of 8 nodes, add a new pool with 8, 16, or 24 nodes.

All drives in the new pool should be of the same type and size within the new pool. Review HyperVault’s hardware recommendations for more complete guidance on selecting an appropriate configuration.

To provide BC-DR grade failover and recovery support for your single or multi-pool HyperVault clusters, use site replication.

Considerations

Minimum stripe size

HyperVault requires that each pool satisfy the cluster erasure code setting as set by the first pool.

The new pool must support the configured parity of all other pools in the cluster as EC:M * 2 drives per erasure set. For example, consider a cluster with a single pool and parity of EC:4. The new expansion pool must support at least 4*2 drives per erasure set.

You can use HyperVault’s Erasure Code Calculator to check the Erasure Code Stripe Size (K+M) of your new pool. Use mc admin info to retrieve the cluster’s EC:M value.

Expanding existing nodes
You cannot expand a server pool by adding drives to an existing node.

Deployments with mixed pool-level stripe sizes can have different object SLAs per pool. A pool with an 8-drive erasure code stripe and EC:4 has distinct read/write quorum behavior than a pool with 12-drive erasure code stripe and EC:4.

HyperVault strongly encourages architecture review from HyperVault Engineering through SUBNET early in the expansion process to analyze and mitigate performance or behavioral impacts.

Writing files

HyperVault does not automatically rebalance objects across the new server pools. Instead, HyperVault performs new write operations to the pool with the most free storage weighted by the amount of free space on the pool divided by the free space across all available pools.

The formula to determine the probability of a write operation on a particular pool is

$$FreeSpaceOnPoolA / FreeSpaceOnAllPools$$

Consider a situation where a group of three pools has a total of 10 TiB of free space distributed as:

  • Pool A has 3 TiB of free space
  • Pool B has 2 TiB of free space
  • Pool C has 5 TiB of free space

HyperVault calculates the probability of a write operation to each of the pools as:

  • Pool A: 30% chance (3TiB / 10TiB)
  • Pool B: 20% chance (2TiB / 10TiB)
  • Pool C: 50% chance (5TiB / 10TiB)

In addition to the free space calculation, if a write operation (with parity) would bring a drive usage above 99% or a known free inode count below 1000, HyperVault does not write to the pool.

If desired, you can manually initiate a rebalance procedure with mc admin rebalance. Finish or stop a rebalance before adding another pool: HyperVault rejects a configuration reload that adds a pool while a rebalance is active.

Likewise, HyperVault does not write to pools in a decommissioning process.

Expansion is non-disruptive

Adding a new server pool requires restarting all Object Store processes in the cluster at around same time.

HyperVault strongly recommends restarting all Object Store processes in a cluster simultaneously. HyperVault operations are atomic and strictly consistent. As such the restart procedure is non-disruptive to applications and ongoing operations.

Do not perform “rolling” (that is, one node at a time) restarts.

Capacity-based planning

HyperVault recommends planning storage capacity sufficient to store at least 2 years of data before reaching 70% usage. Performing server pool expansion more frequently or on a “just-in-time” basis generally indicates an architecture or planning issue.

For example, consider an application suite expected to produce at least 100 TiB of data per year and a 3 year target before expansion. The cluster has ~500TiB of usable storage in the initial server pool, such that the cluster safely met the 70% threshold with some buffer for data growth. The new server pool should ideally meet at minimum 500TiB of additional storage to allow for a similar lifespan before further expansion.

Since HyperVault erasure coding requires some storage for parity, the total raw storage must exceed the planned usable capacity. Consider using the HyperVault Erasure Code Calculator for guidance in planning capacity around specific erasure code settings.

Recommended operating systems

This tutorial assumes all hosts running HyperVault use a recommended Linux operating system.

All hosts in the deployment should run with matching software configurations.

Procedures

Follow the guide for your platform: expand a deployment on Linux or expand a deployment on Kubernetes.
text: Expand Available Storage MinIO AIStor supports expanding an existing distributed cluster by adding a new server pool. Each pool expands the total available storage capacity of the cluster. MinIO AIStor does not support increasing storage through logical volume expansion, rolling drive replacement, or other filesystem-level approaches. Expansion does not provide Business Continuity/Disaster Recovery (BC/DR)-grade protections. While each pool is an independent set of servers with distinct erasure sets for availability, the complete loss of one pool results in MinIO stopping I/O for all pools in the cluster. Similarly, an erasure set which loses quorum in one pool represents data loss of objects stored in that set, regardless of the number of other erasure sets or pools. While MinIO AIStor does not strictly require that the new server pool use the same type or size of hardware and software configuration as any existing server pool, MinIO strongly recommends a similar configuration. This allows for simplified cluster management and more predictable performance across pools. For example, if your existing cluster has a pool of 8 nodes, add a new pool with 8, 16, or 24 nodes. All drives in the new pool should be of the same type and size within the new pool. Review MinIO’s hardware recommendations for more complete guidance on selecting an appropriate configuration. To provide BC-DR grade failover and recovery support for your single or multi-pool MinIO AIStor clusters, use site replication. Considerations Minimum stripe size MinIO AIStor requires that each pool satisfy the cluster erasure code setting as set by the first pool. The new pool must support the configured parity of all other pools in the cluster as EC:M * 2 drives per erasure set. For example, consider a cluster with a single pool and parity of EC:4. The new expansion pool must support at least 4*2 drives per erasure set. You can use MinIO’s Erasure Code Calculator to check the Erasure Code Stripe Size (K+M) of your new pool. Use mc admin info to retrieve the cluster’s EC:M value. Expanding existing nodes You cannot expand a server pool by adding drives to an existing node. Deployments with mixed pool-level stripe sizes can have different object SLAs per pool. A pool with an 8-drive erasure code stripe and EC:4 has distinct read/write quorum behavior than a pool with 12-drive erasure code stripe and EC:4. MinIO strongly encourages architecture review from MinIO Engineering through SUBNET early in the expansion process to analyze and mitigate performance or behavioral impacts. Writing files MinIO AIStor does not automatically rebalance objects across the new server pools. Instead, MinIO AIStor performs new write operations to the pool with the most free storage weighted by the amount of free space on the pool divided by the free space across all available pools. The formula to determine the probability of a write operation on a particular pool is $$FreeSpaceOnPoolA / FreeSpaceOnAllPools$$Consider a situation where a group of three pools has a total of 10 TiB of free space distributed as: Pool A has 3 TiB of free space Pool B has 2 TiB of free space Pool C has 5 TiB of free space MinIO AIStor calculates the probability of a write operation to each of the pools as: Pool A: 30% chance (3TiB / 10TiB) Pool B: 20% chance (2TiB / 10TiB) Pool C: 50% chance (5TiB / 10TiB) In addition to the free space calculation, if a write operation (with parity) would bring a drive usage above 99% or a known free inode count below 1000, MinIO AIStor does not write to the pool. If desired, you can manually initiate a rebalance procedure with mc admin rebalance. Finish or stop a rebalance before adding another pool: MinIO AIStor rejects a configuration reload that adds a pool while a rebalance is active. Likewise, MinIO does not write to pools in a decommissioning process. Expansion is non-disruptive Adding a new server pool requires restarting all Object Store processes in the cluster at around same time. MinIO strongly recommends restarting all Object Store processes in a cluster simultaneously. MinIO AIStor operations are atomic and strictly consistent. As such the restart procedure is non-disruptive to applications and ongoing operations. Do not perform “rolling” (that is, one node at a time) restarts. Capacity-based planning MinIO recommends planning storage capacity sufficient to store at least 2 years of data before reaching 70% usage. Performing server pool expansion more frequently or on a “just-in-time” basis generally indicates an architecture or planning issue. For example, consider an application suite expected to produce at least 100 TiB of data per year and a 3 year target before expansion. The cluster has ~500TiB of usable storage in the initial server pool, such that the cluster safely met the 70% threshold with some buffer for data growth. The new server pool should ideally meet at minimum 500TiB of additional storage to allow for a similar lifespan before further expansion. Since MinIO AIStor erasure coding requires some storage for parity, the total raw storage must exceed the planned usable capacity. Consider using the MinIO Erasure Code Calculator for guidance in planning capacity around specific erasure code settings. Recommended operating systems This tutorial assumes all hosts running MinIO use a recommended Linux operating system. All hosts in the deployment should run with matching software configurations. Procedures Follow the guide for your platform: expand a deployment on Linux or expand a deployment on Kubernetes.

title: Expand a HyperVault Deployment on Kubernetes | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Expand a HyperVault Deployment on Kubernetes

The following procedure adds a server pool to an existing HyperVault cluster running on Kubernetes infrastructure. Each pool expands the total available storage capacity of the cluster with new nodes and persistent volumes while maintaining the overall availability of the cluster. Pay particular attention to the parity (EC:M) value of the existing cluster and the new pool.

HyperVault strongly recommends seeking an architecture review from HyperVault Engineering through SUBNET to analyze potential performance impacts before committing to a new pool for your cluster.

All commands provided below use example values. Replace these values with those appropriate for your cluster.

  1. Retrieve and review the existing object store Helm chart.

    The objectStore.pools key describes the current cluster’s topology and pool configuration. Each element in the pools array describes a single server pool in the HyperVault cluster.

    Review this file and take a timestamped backup as object-store-NAME-values.yaml.TIMESTAMP-bak before proceeding.

  2. Prepare new worker nodes.

    Add or configure the new worker nodes for supporting HyperVault. Ensure the worker nodes have the necessary storage and compute resources for supporting the target architecture.

  3. Modify the objectStore.pools array with the new pool.

    The following example adds a new pool pool-1 to an existing cluster with a single pool pool-0. Each pool uses a nodeSelector to restrict the cluster to specific worker nodes based on label:

    objectStore:
   name: primary-object-store # name of the HyperVault Server
   pools:
   - name: pool-0
     servers: 8 # Number of servers/pods to deploy
     volumesPerServer: 8 # Number of Persistent Volumes per Server/Pod
     size: 2Ti # Size of each PV
     storageClassName: directpv-min-io # Storage Class assigned to each PV
     nodeSelector: {
       hypervault-label: "primary-object-store-pool-0"

     }
   - name: pool-1
     servers: 32
     volumesPerServer: 32
     size: 2Ti
     storageClassName: directpv-min-io
     nodeSelector: {
       hypervault-label: "primary-object-store-pool-1"
     }
   services:
      hypervault:
         serviceType: NodePort
         nodePort: 31000 # Select an available NodePort in the supported range of 30000-32767

  4. Deploy the chart with the updated values.

    Use the helm upgrade command to upgrade the chart with the new values.yaml:

    helm upgrade primary-object-store hypervault/hypervault-objectstore \
  -n hypervault-primary-object-store \
  -f primary-object-store-values.yaml

    You can use kubectl get events -n NAMESPACE --watch to monitor the progress of expansion.

    Once the expansion completes, use the mc admin info command to validate the expanded topology and status.

Next steps

After validating cluster health and expanded storage, you can update any load balancers, reverse proxies, or other network management tools with the new hostnames of the added server pool. This ensures that incoming connections balance appropriately across the expanded topology.

title: Expand a HyperVault Deployment on Linux | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Expand a HyperVault Deployment on Linux

The following procedures add a server pool to an existing HyperVault cluster running on bare-metal infrastructure. Each pool expands the total available storage capacity of the cluster while maintaining the overall availability of the cluster.

A new pool is a set of new nodes and drives that meet the cluster’s erasure set requirements and parity levels.

You can use HyperVault’s Erasure Code Calculator to check the Erasure Code Stripe Size (K+M) of your new pool to confirm that it meets the EC:M value of the current cluster. HyperVault strongly recommends seeking an architecture review from HyperVault Engineering through SUBNET to analyze potential performance impacts before committing to a new pool for your cluster.

All commands provided below use example values. Replace these values with those appropriate for your cluster.

Pool Hot-Reload (Configuration File Method)

This method requires that your cluster uses a configuration file with the --config flag. If your cluster uses environment variables or command-line arguments to define pools, use the environment variable method instead.

The pool hot-reload method adds storage pools to a running cluster without restarting the server. This method uses SIGHUP to trigger a configuration reload, allowing the cluster to detect and integrate new pools dynamically.

Requires HyperVault RELEASE.2026-02-02T23-40-11Z or later.

Stop any active rebalance first

HyperVault rejects a configuration reload that adds a pool while a rebalance is active. Run mc admin rebalance status ALIAS to check, and mc admin rebalance stop ALIAS to stop one before you proceed.

The systemctl reload command still succeeds when the reload is rejected. HyperVault reports the rejection in the server log rather than to the shell, so confirm the outcome in the log rather than assuming the reload applied.

  1. Deploy HyperVault on new hardware.

    Follow the installation guide to install HyperVault onto the new hardware.

    Do not start the new cluster - stop at the step Review the environment file.

  2. Update the configuration file.

    On one of the existing cluster nodes, edit the configuration file to add the new pool to the pools array.

    For example, if your current configuration defines a single pool:

    version: v2
address: ":9000"
console-address: ":9001"
rootUser: "hypervaultadmin"
rootPassword: "secret-CHANGE-ME"
pools:
  - args:
      - "https://hypervault-{1...16}.example.net:9000/mnt/drive-{1...16}/hypervault"

    Add a second pool by appending another entry to the pools array:

    version: v2
address: ":9000"
console-address: ":9001"
rootUser: "hypervaultadmin"
rootPassword: "secret-CHANGE-ME"
pools:
  - args:
      - "https://hypervault-{1...16}.example.net:9000/mnt/drive-{1...16}/hypervault"
  - args:
      - "https://hypervault-{17...32}.example.net:9000/mnt/drive-{1...16}/hypervault"

    Append new pools at the end of the list of existing pools. The order of existing pools must be preserved.

    Save the file and copy the updated configuration file to all nodes in the cluster, including both existing and new pool nodes. Use shasum or a similar utility to confirm that the configuration matches on all existing and new nodes.

  3. Start the new pool nodes.

    On the new pool nodes, start the HyperVault service:

    systemctl start hypervault

  4. Trigger the configuration reload on the existing pool nodes.

    The new pool nodes already start with the updated configuration, so no reload is required on those nodes. Reload the HyperVault service on each node in the existing cluster to pick up the new pool:

    systemctl reload hypervault

    To run the reload across every existing node in one shot, use clush or an equivalent parallel-SSH tool:

    clush -w @storage-nodes "systemctl reload hypervault"

    Each existing node reloads its configuration independently and integrates the new pool once all nodes have reloaded successfully.

  5. Monitor the cluster status.

    Use the mc admin info command to verify the new pool appears in the cluster:

    mc admin info ALIAS

    Monitor the server logs on all nodes to observe the pool addition process:

    journalctl -u hypervault -f

    The logs should show messages indicating the new pool was successfully integrated.

  6. Next steps

    After validating cluster health and expanded storage, update any load balancers, reverse proxies, or other network management tools with the new hostnames of the added server pool. This ensures that incoming connections balance appropriately across the expanded topology.

Environment Variable Method

This method requires restarting the cluster to apply the new pool configuration.

  1. Deploy HyperVault on new hardware.

    Follow the installation guide to install HyperVault onto the new hardware.

    Do not start the new cluster - stop at the step Review the environment file

  2. Update the cluster topology.

    HyperVault uses the HYPERVAULT_VOLUMES environment variable for determining the cluster topology.

    When adding a new pool, append the new set of hostnames and volumes to the existing set. For example, consider the following HYPERVAULT_VOLUMES describing a single-pool consisting of 16 nodes and 16 drives:

    HYPERVAULT_VOLUMES="https://hypervault-{1...16}.example.net:9000/mnt/drive-{1...16}/hypervault"

    To expand that topology with another 16x16 cluster, append the new set of hosts to the existing value:

    HYPERVAULT_VOLUMES="https://hypervault-{1...16}.example.net:9000/mnt/drive-{1...16}/hypervault https://hypervault-{17...32}.example.net:9000/mnt/drive-{1...16}/hypervault"

    You must include the protocol http[s]:// for each new pool. All pools should have matching protocols.

    Make this change to all hosts in the HyperVault cluster, including the existing pools. The environment files should match across all nodes. Use shasum or a similar utility to validate that all contents match.

  3. Initialize the new cluster topology.

    You must simultaneously

    1. Restart the existing HyperVault cluster and
    2. Start the new HyperVault server nodes

    For the existing nodes, you can use the mc admin service restart command to restart all nodes at once. For the new nodes, use systemctl start hypervault on all nodes in parallel using your preferred shell tooling.

  4. Monitor the cluster status.

    Use the mc admin info command and journalctl -u hypervault system utility to monitor status and logging across the cluster. While the nodes come online and synchronize, the system logs may showcase increased churn through warnings and errors.

  5. Next steps

    After validating cluster health and expanded storage, update any load balancers, reverse proxies, or other network management tools with the new hostnames of the added server pool. This ensures that incoming connections balance appropriately across the expanded topology.

title: Storage Hardening | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Storage Hardening

HyperVault supports kernel-level storage protection to prevent accidental deletion of data directories by system administrators while allowing the HyperVault process full control over managed drives. This protection is critical for production environments where a mistyped rm -rf /drive* command could result in catastrophic data loss.

Protection model

Storage hardening provides:

  • HyperVault process: Full read/write/delete access to managed drives.
  • Host OS (including root): Cannot delete protected data. With SELinux, other processes have read-only access to protected directories. With eBPF LSM, other processes are blocked from deleting or renaming files owned by a protected UID.
  • Kernel-level enforcement: Protection cannot be bypassed through normal filesystem operations.
  • No performance impact: Both implementations add negligible overhead.

Choose an implementation

HyperVault provides two storage protection implementations:

Feature SELinux eBPF LSM
Kernel version Any (built into most enterprise distros) Supported on all HyperVault-compatible kernels
Best for RHEL, CentOS, Fedora Ubuntu, Debian, other distros
Configuration Policy files and labels Kernel parameter + daemon
Protection model File labels (hypervault_data_t) File ownership (UID allowlist)
Maturity 20+ years in production Newer, but production-ready

Recommendations:

  • RHEL/CentOS/Fedora: Use SELinux (better integration, native support)
  • Ubuntu/Debian: Use eBPF LSM (default kernel support, no SELinux required)
  • Other distributions: Use eBPF LSM for universal compatibility

SELinux-based protection

Use SELinux-based storage protection on RHEL, CentOS, Fedora, and other SELinux-enabled systems.

Prerequisites

  • RHEL 8/9, CentOS 8/9, Fedora, or any Linux distribution with SELinux.
  • SELinux in enforcing or permissive mode (not disabled).
  • SELinux policy development tools.

Check SELinux status:

getenforce

The output should be Enforcing or Permissive. If the output is Disabled, enable SELinux first:

# Edit SELinux config
sudo vi /etc/selinux/config

# Set SELINUX=enforcing
SELINUX=enforcing

# Reboot required
sudo reboot

Install required tools:

sudo dnf install -y policycoreutils-python-utils selinux-policy-devel

Setup

Follow these steps to create and install the SELinux policy.

Create the SELinux policy module

Create a file named hypervault_storage.te:

policy_module(hypervault_storage, 1.0.0)

require {
    type unconfined_t;
    type user_t;
    type sysadm_t;
    type init_t;
    class dir { add_name create getattr ioctl link lock open read remove_name rename reparent rmdir search setattr unlink watch watch_reads write };
    class file { append create getattr ioctl link lock map open read rename setattr unlink write };
}

# Define HyperVault domain
type hypervault_t;
type hypervault_exec_t;
type hypervault_data_t;

# HyperVault binary type
files_type(hypervault_exec_t)

# HyperVault data directories type
files_type(hypervault_data_t)

# Allow HyperVault domain to be entered from init
init_daemon_domain(hypervault_t, hypervault_exec_t)
domain_type(hypervault_t)

# HyperVault process has FULL access to hypervault_data_t
allow hypervault_t hypervault_data_t:dir { add_name create getattr ioctl link lock open read remove_name rename reparent rmdir search setattr unlink watch watch_reads write };
allow hypervault_t hypervault_data_t:file { append create getattr ioctl link lock map open read rename setattr unlink write };

# All other processes can ONLY read, CANNOT delete or write
allow unconfined_t hypervault_data_t:dir { getattr open read search };
allow unconfined_t hypervault_data_t:file { getattr open read };
allow user_t hypervault_data_t:dir { getattr open read search };
allow user_t hypervault_data_t:file { getattr open read };
allow sysadm_t hypervault_data_t:dir { getattr open read search };
allow sysadm_t hypervault_data_t:file { getattr open read };

# HyperVault network access
corenet_tcp_bind_generic_node(hypervault_t)
corenet_tcp_connect_http_port(hypervault_t)
corenet_tcp_bind_http_port(hypervault_t)
corenet_tcp_bind_generic_port(hypervault_t)
corenet_udp_bind_generic_port(hypervault_t)

# HyperVault system permissions
kernel_read_system_state(hypervault_t)
dev_read_urand(hypervault_t)
fs_getattr_xattr_fs(hypervault_t)
files_read_etc_files(hypervault_t)
miscfiles_read_localization(hypervault_t)
sysnet_dns_name_resolve(hypervault_t)

# Allow HyperVault to execute itself
allow hypervault_t hypervault_exec_t:file { execute execute_no_trans getattr map open read };

Compile and install the policy 

# Compile the policy module
checkmodule -M -m -o hypervault_storage.mod hypervault_storage.te

# Package the module
semodule_package -o hypervault_storage.pp -m hypervault_storage.mod

# Install the policy module
semodule -i hypervault_storage.pp

# Verify installation
semodule -l | grep hypervault_storage

Label the HyperVault binary 

# Set file context for HyperVault binary
semanage fcontext -a -t hypervault_exec_t "/usr/local/bin/hypervault"

# Apply the label
restorecon -v /usr/local/bin/hypervault

# Verify the label
ls -Z /usr/local/bin/hypervault

The output should show system_u:object_r:hypervault_exec_t:s0.

Label data directories

For each drive that HyperVault manages:

# Add file context rules for each drive
semanage fcontext -a -t hypervault_data_t "/drive1(/.*)?"
semanage fcontext -a -t hypervault_data_t "/drive2(/.*)?"
semanage fcontext -a -t hypervault_data_t "/drive3(/.*)?"
semanage fcontext -a -t hypervault_data_t "/drive4(/.*)?"

# Apply labels recursively
restorecon -R -v /drive1 /drive2 /drive3 /drive4

# Verify labels
ls -Z /drive1

The output should show system_u:object_r:hypervault_data_t:s0.

Verify SELinux protection

Test that protection is working:

# Create a test file (as HyperVault or with proper context)
sudo -u hypervault-user touch /drive1/test-file

# Try to delete as root (should fail)
sudo rm /drive1/test-file
# Expected: rm: cannot remove '/drive1/...': Permission denied

Check that processes are running in the correct SELinux domain:

# Check HyperVault process context
ps -eZ | grep hypervault
# Expected: system_u:system_r:hypervault_t:s0

# Check file contexts
ls -Z /drive1
# Expected: system_u:object_r:hypervault_data_t:s0

eBPF LSM-based protection

Use eBPF LSM-based storage protection on Ubuntu, Debian, and other distributions without SELinux.

Prerequisites

  • HyperVault-compatible Linux kernel with eBPF LSM support.
  • CONFIG_BPF_LSM=y kernel configuration.
  • lsm=...,bpf kernel boot parameter.
  • Root access for installation.

Check kernel support:

# Check kernel version
uname -r

# Check if eBPF LSM is enabled
cat /sys/kernel/security/lsm | grep -q bpf && echo "Supported" || echo "Not supported"

# Check kernel configuration (if available)
grep CONFIG_BPF_LSM /boot/config-$(uname -r)

Enable eBPF LSM

If eBPF LSM is not in the LSM list, enable it via kernel boot parameters.

# Edit GRUB configuration
sudo vi /etc/default/grub

# Add or modify GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT="quiet splash lsm=lockdown,yama,integrity,apparmor,bpf"

# Update GRUB
sudo update-grub

# Reboot
sudo reboot

# Edit GRUB configuration
sudo vi /etc/default/grub

# Add or modify GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="... lsm=selinux,bpf"

# Update GRUB
sudo grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg

# Reboot
sudo reboot

Install required packages 

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y \
    clang \
    llvm \
    libbpf-dev \
    linux-tools-generic \
    linux-headers-$(uname -r) \
    golang-go

sudo dnf install -y \
    clang \
    llvm \
    libbpf-devel \
    bpftool \
    kernel-devel \
    golang

How eBPF protection works

The hypervault-lsm-bpf daemon uses a pure UID-based protection model. You pass it one or more UIDs to protect using the -u option, typically the UID of the user that runs HyperVault. The daemon then protects all files owned by those UIDs, regardless of their location on disk:

  1. The daemon attaches eBPF programs to the kernel LSM hooks.
  2. When a process attempts to delete a file, the hook checks whether the file is owned by a protected UID.
  3. If the file is owned by a protected UID, the operation is allowed only when the deleting process runs as the same UID.
  4. All other processes, including root, are blocked from deleting files owned by a protected UID.

The eBPF LSM hooks intercept:

  • unlink() - File deletion.
  • rmdir() - Directory deletion.
  • rename() - Moving or renaming files.

Because protection is based on file ownership rather than path, any drive whose files are owned by a protected UID is covered automatically.

Setup

Follow these steps to build, install, and run the protection daemon from the scripts/ebpf directory of the HyperVault source tree.

Verify kernel support 

# Check eBPF LSM support
if ! cat /sys/kernel/security/lsm | grep -q bpf; then
    echo "eBPF LSM not enabled - add 'bpf' to kernel boot parameters"
    exit 1
fi

echo "Kernel support: OK"

You can also run make check-kernel from the scripts/ebpf directory to verify that the system is ready.

Build the eBPF program 

cd scripts/ebpf

# Verify the required build tools are present
make check-tools

# Build the binary (default 'all' target)
make

# Verify the binary was created
ls -lh hypervault-lsm-bpf

Install the binary 

# Install to system path
sudo install -m 0755 hypervault-lsm-bpf /usr/local/bin/

Create the systemd service

Determine the UID that HyperVault runs as:

# Get the UID of hypervault-user (for example, 1000)
id -u hypervault-user

Create /etc/systemd/system/hypervault-lsm-bpf.service, replacing 1000 with the UID from the previous command:

[Unit]
Description=HyperVault eBPF LSM Protection
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/hypervault-lsm-bpf -u 1000
Restart=always
RestartSec=10
LimitMEMLOCK=infinity
StandardOutput=journal
StandardError=journal

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

To protect more than one UID, repeat the -u option, for example ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/hypervault-lsm-bpf -u 1000 -u 1001.

The daemon supports the following options:

  • -u UID - UID whose files are protected (required, can be repeated).
  • -v - Enable verbose logging (logs allowed operations in addition to blocked operations).

Enable and start the service 

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now hypervault-lsm-bpf
sudo systemctl status hypervault-lsm-bpf

Verify eBPF protection

Test that protection is working:

# Create a test file owned by the protected user
sudo -u hypervault-user touch /drive1/test-file

# Try to delete as root (should fail)
sudo rm /drive1/test-file
# Expected: rm: cannot remove '/drive1/test-file': Operation not permitted

# Verify the file still exists
ls -l /drive1/test-file

# Delete as the file owner (should succeed)
sudo -u hypervault-user rm /drive1/test-file

Check service status:

# Service status
sudo systemctl status hypervault-lsm-bpf

# View logs (blocked operations appear in real time)
sudo journalctl -u hypervault-lsm-bpf -f
# Example output:
# BLOCKED unlink: op_pid=1234 op_uid=0 comm=rm owner_uid=1000

Troubleshooting

HyperVault cannot start

If HyperVault fails to start after enabling protection:

# Check SELinux denials
sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent

# Check HyperVault binary label
ls -Z /usr/local/bin/hypervault

# Temporarily set permissive mode to diagnose
sudo setenforce 0
# Start HyperVault, then check audit log
sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent | audit2allow

# Check if the hypervault-lsm-bpf service is running
sudo systemctl status hypervault-lsm-bpf

# Check logs for errors
sudo journalctl -u hypervault-lsm-bpf -n 50

# Verify kernel support
cat /sys/kernel/security/lsm | grep -q bpf && echo "Supported" || echo "Not supported"

# Restart protection service
sudo systemctl restart hypervault-lsm-bpf

HyperVault cannot write to drives

If HyperVault cannot write to protected drives:

# Verify directory labels
ls -Z /drive1

# Relabel if needed
restorecon -R -v /drive1

# Check for context mismatches
sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent | grep hypervault

The daemon only blocks deletions of files owned by a protected UID; it never blocks the owning UID from writing or deleting its own files. If HyperVault cannot write to a drive, confirm that the drive’s files are owned by the UID that HyperVault runs as and that this UID matches the one passed with -u.

# Confirm the protected UID matches the HyperVault user
id -u hypervault-user
sudo systemctl show hypervault-lsm-bpf -p ExecStart

# Confirm drive ownership
ls -ln /drive1

# Check logs for blocked operations
sudo journalctl -u hypervault-lsm-bpf -n 50

Protection not blocking root

If root can still delete files:

# Verify SELinux is enforcing
getenforce

# Check if policy is loaded
semodule -l | grep hypervault_storage

# Verify file contexts
ls -Z /drive1

# Verify eBPF program is loaded
sudo bpftool prog list | grep hypervault

# Verify LSM hooks are attached
sudo bpftool link list

# Check the service logs for blocked operations
sudo journalctl -u hypervault-lsm-bpf | grep BLOCKED

Security considerations

Defense in depth

Storage hardening is one layer of defense. Implement additional measures:

  • Regular backups to separate storage
  • Filesystem snapshots (ZFS, Btrfs, LVM)
  • Restricted SSH access with key-based authentication
  • Multi-factor authentication for administrative access
  • Monitoring for unauthorized access attempts

Limitations

Both implementations have known limitations:

Limitation Mitigation
Root can disable the protection service Monitor service status, use systemd protections
Root can change kernel parameters via reboot Use TPM/UEFI Secure Boot to protect boot parameters
Direct block device access bypasses filesystem Use disk encryption, monitor block device access

Adding new drives

When adding new drives, label them with the correct SELinux context:

semanage fcontext -a -t hypervault_data_t "/drive9(/.*)?"
restorecon -R -v /drive9

eBPF protection is based on file ownership, not path. Any drive whose files are owned by a protected UID is covered automatically, regardless of its mount path. No configuration changes are needed when adding a drive, provided its files are owned by an already-protected UID.

To protect files owned by an additional UID, add another -u UID argument to the daemon’s ExecStart line and restart the service:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart hypervault-lsm-bpf

Uninstalling 

# Remove the policy module
sudo semodule -r hypervault_storage

# Remove file context rules
sudo semanage fcontext -d "/usr/local/bin/hypervault"
sudo semanage fcontext -d "/drive1(/.*)?"
# Repeat for other drives

# Restore default labels
sudo restorecon -R -v /usr/local/bin/hypervault /drive1

sudo systemctl disable --now hypervault-lsm-bpf
sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/hypervault-lsm-bpf.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo rm /usr/local/bin/hypervault-lsm-bpf

With SELinux, other processes have read-only access to protected directories. With eBPF LSM, other processes are blocked from deleting or renaming files owned by a protected UID. title: Software Lifecycle and End-of-Life | HyperVault Documentation
html:
Software Lifecycle and End-of-Life

Last updated: August 28, 2026.

This page defines the HyperVault software support lifecycle and End-of-Life (EOL) policy, the operating systems and architectures HyperVault runs on, the S3 API surface it implements, and the client SDKs HyperVault maintains. Support terms depend on your subscription tier. See HyperVault Pricing for tier details.

Release lifecycle and End-of-Life

This section defines how long a given HyperVault release is supported and maintained, and when it reaches End of Life.

Definitions

  • Release — A published, versioned build of HyperVault, identified by its release tag RELEASE.YYYY-MM-DDTHH-MM-SSZ.
  • Current release — The latest release published by HyperVault at any given point in time.
  • Support term — The window, measured from a release’s publication date, during which that release is eligible for maintenance under your tier.
  • Hotfix — A hotfix release backports a security, regression, or critical-bug fix to a specific release tag so a production deployment can stay on its standardized version and still receive the fix.
  • EOL / void — Once a release reaches End of Life for your tier, it is void: it receives no further fixes, security patches, or hotfixes and is no longer eligible for support. Continued use is at your own risk. Remaining supported requires upgrading to a release that is current at the time of upgrade.

Policy by tier

Tier Support term per release Hotfixes to your deployed release Upgrade obligation
Enterprise Lite 12 months (1-year LTS) None — upgrade forward for fixes Upgrade to a current release before your deployed release’s 12-month term ends
Enterprise 24 months (2-year LTS) Yes, for the full 24-month term Upgrade to a current release before your deployed release’s 24-month term ends

Enterprise Lite — 1-year LTS

Each release carries a 12-month support term from its publication date. Fixes are delivered in newer releases: to receive a security or critical-bug fix, upgrade to a release that is current at the time of the upgrade. Hotfix backports to a pinned production version are not included at the Enterprise Lite tier.

A release you run today must be upgraded, before its 12-month term closes, to a release that is current at the time of that upgrade. Once you upgrade, the prior release becomes void.

Enterprise — 2-year LTS

HyperVault supports any released version for up to a 2-year Long-Term Support (LTS) term. Each release carries a 24-month support term from its publication date, and hotfixes backport fixes to the exact release you run in production, so you can remain on a standardized release for up to two years and still receive fixes without a forced version jump.

Support commitments for LTS releases include:

  • Security patches — CVE remediations and vulnerability disclosures.
  • Critical and high-severity bug fixes — stability and data-integrity issues.
  • Predictable EOL date — a release’s end of maintenance is fixed at its release date plus two years, giving each release a known, plannable end-of-maintenance date.

As with Enterprise Lite, a release you run today must be upgraded, before its 24-month term closes, to a release that is current at the time of that upgrade. The prior release then becomes void.

Enterprise customers are encouraged to engage HyperVault support through the SUBNET portal for lifecycle guidance, upgrade planning, and prioritized security advisories ahead of public disclosure.

Worked example

Assume you deploy RELEASE.2026-01-15T..., the current release on the day you deploy it.

  • Enterprise Lite — RELEASE.2026-01-15T... is supported through 2027-01-15. To receive a fix during that window, upgrade to the then-current release. Before 2027-01-15 you must upgrade to a current release; the prior release is then void.
  • Enterprise — RELEASE.2026-01-15T... is supported through 2028-01-15, with hotfixes backported to it for the full two years. Before 2028-01-15 you must upgrade to a then-current release; the prior release is then void.
Plan upgrades early
HyperVault recommends staying reasonably close to the current release regardless of tier, both to minimize the size of any single upgrade and to benefit from performance and feature improvements between releases. Enterprise subscribers should coordinate lifecycle planning with their HyperVault account team. See Upgrade for procedures.
Policy subject to change
HyperVault reserves the right to modify this lifecycle and LTS policy to meet business requirements. Material changes are reflected on this page; refer to the last-updated date at the top for the current revision.

Operating system compatibility

HyperVault runs on 64-bit Linux and is regularly validated across the Enterprise Linux, Ubuntu LTS, and SUSE Linux Enterprise families below.

HyperVault recommends a 6.8.x or newer kernel for all new deployments. Older 4.x and 5.x kernels — such as those shipped with RHEL 8 and Ubuntu 20.04 — run HyperVault and remain supported, but modern workloads and high-performance NVMe drives demand newer kernels to operate at peak efficiency. A 6.8+ kernel unlocks critical performance features; where possible, bring older hosts to a 6.8+ kernel (for example, through a vendor hardware-enablement kernel) before production use.

Older kernels bottleneck modern hardware
Pairing a 4.x or 5.x kernel with current-generation hardware measurably degrades performance. Older kernels lack the storage and network stack improvements needed to drive the latest devices at their rated throughput — for example, the newest PCIe Gen5 NVMe drives and 400GbE network adapters. On such hardware, an older kernel becomes the bottleneck: HyperVault cannot reach peak IOPS or line-rate network throughput until the host runs a 6.8+ kernel.
Distribution family Version Default kernel Guidance for new deployments
RHEL / Rocky Linux / AlmaLinux / Oracle Linux 8 4.18 Supported; 6.8+ recommended
9 5.14 Supported; 6.8+ recommended
10 6.12 Recommended
Ubuntu LTS 20.04 5.4 Supported; 6.8+ recommended
22.04 5.15 Supported; 6.8+ recommended
24.04 6.8 Recommended
SUSE Linux Enterprise 15 SP7 6.4 Supported; 6.8+ recommended

See the software checklist for the full pre-deployment software requirements.

Architectures

HyperVault ships for the AMD64 (x86-64) and ARM64 (aarch64) architectures, distributed as .rpm, .deb, and container images.

Filesystem

Drives must be formatted with the XFS filesystem for the performance and consistency guarantees HyperVault depends on. Do not use ext4 or NFS for distributed deployments.

S3 API compatibility

The HyperVault Object API is S3-compatible and a drop-in replacement for Amazon S3 across the documented operations, so existing S3 applications and tooling work against HyperVault without changes. Supported object operations include CopyObject, DeleteObject, DeleteObjects, GetObject, GetObjectAttributes, HeadObject, ListObjects, ListObjectsV2, ListObjectVersions, PutObject, RestoreObject, SelectObjectContent, object tagging, conditional headers (If-Match, If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, If-Unmodified-Since), and object locking, retention, and legal hold.

Per-object ACL operations (GetObjectAcl, PutObjectAcl) are not supported: HyperVault uses policy-based access control rather than per-object ACLs.

For the full, authoritative list of supported and unsupported APIs, see S3 API Compatibility.

Client SDKs

HyperVault maintains official, S3-compatible client SDKs across the following languages. Each targets the same S3 API surface, so applications are portable across languages.

Language SDK repository
Go hypervault/hypervault-go
Python hypervault/hypervault-py
Java hypervault/hypervault-java
JavaScript hypervault/hypervault-js
.NET hypervault/hypervault-dotnet
C++ hypervault/hypervault-cpp
Haskell hypervault/hypervault-hs
Rust hypervault/hypervault-rs

Because the API is S3-compatible, standard AWS SDKs (for example, boto3, aws-sdk-go, aws-sdk-java) and the AWS CLI also work against HyperVault. See the SDK documentation for quickstarts and API references.
text: Software Lifecycle and End-of-Life Last updated: August 28, 2026. This page defines the MinIO AIStor software support lifecycle and End-of-Life (EOL) policy, the operating systems and architectures AIStor runs on, the S3 API surface it implements, and the client SDKs MinIO maintains. Support terms depend on your subscription tier. See MinIO Pricing for tier details. Release lifecycle and End-of-Life This section defines how long a given MinIO AIStor release is supported and maintained, and when it reaches End of Life. Definitions Release — A published, versioned build of MinIO AIStor, identified by its release tag RELEASE.YYYY-MM-DDTHH-MM-SSZ. Current release — The latest release published by MinIO at any given point in time. Support term — The window, measured from a release’s publication date, during which that release is eligible for maintenance under your tier. Hotfix — A hotfix release backports a security, regression, or critical-bug fix to a specific release tag so a production deployment can stay on its standardized version and still receive the fix. EOL / void — Once a release reaches End of Life for your tier, it is void: it receives no further fixes, security patches, or hotfixes and is no longer eligible for support. Continued use is at your own risk. Remaining supported requires upgrading to a release that is current at the time of upgrade. Policy by tier Tier Support term per release Hotfixes to your deployed release Upgrade obligation Enterprise Lite 12 months (1-year LTS) None — upgrade forward for fixes Upgrade to a current release before your deployed release’s 12-month term ends Enterprise 24 months (2-year LTS) Yes, for the full 24-month term Upgrade to a current release before your deployed release’s 24-month term ends Enterprise Lite — 1-year LTS Each release carries a 12-month support term from its publication date. Fixes are delivered in newer releases: to receive a security or critical-bug fix, upgrade to a release that is current at the time of the upgrade. Hotfix backports to a pinned production version are not included at the Enterprise Lite tier. A release you run today must be upgraded, before its 12-month term closes, to a release that is current at the time of that upgrade. Once you upgrade, the prior release becomes void. Enterprise — 2-year LTS MinIO supports any released version for up to a 2-year Long-Term Support (LTS) term. Each release carries a 24-month support term from its publication date, and hotfixes backport fixes to the exact release you run in production, so you can remain on a standardized release for up to two years and still receive fixes without a forced version jump. Support commitments for LTS releases include: Security patches — CVE remediations and vulnerability disclosures. Critical and high-severity bug fixes — stability and data-integrity issues. Predictable EOL date — a release’s end of maintenance is fixed at its release date plus two years, giving each release a known, plannable end-of-maintenance date. As with Enterprise Lite, a release you run today must be upgraded, before its 24-month term closes, to a release that is current at the time of that upgrade. The prior release then becomes void. Enterprise customers are encouraged to engage MinIO support through the SUBNET portal for lifecycle guidance, upgrade planning, and prioritized security advisories ahead of public disclosure. Worked example Assume you deploy RELEASE.2026-01-15T..., the current release on the day you deploy it. Enterprise Lite — RELEASE.2026-01-15T... is supported through 2027-01-15. To receive a fix during that window, upgrade to the then-current release. Before 2027-01-15 you must upgrade to a current release; the prior release is then void. Enterprise — RELEASE.2026-01-15T... is supported through 2028-01-15, with hotfixes backported to it for the full two years. Before 2028-01-15 you must upgrade to a then-current release; the prior release is then void. Plan upgrades early MinIO recommends staying reasonably close to the current release regardless of tier, both to minimize the size of any single upgrade and to benefit from performance and feature improvements between releases. Enterprise subscribers should coordinate lifecycle planning with their MinIO account team. See Upgrade for procedures. Policy subject to change MinIO reserves the right to modify this lifecycle and LTS policy to meet business requirements. Material changes are reflected on this page; refer to the last-updated date at the top for the current revision. Operating system compatibility MinIO AIStor runs on 64-bit Linux and is regularly validated across the Enterprise Linux, Ubuntu LTS, and SUSE Linux Enterprise families below. MinIO recommends a 6.8.x or newer kernel for all new deployments. Older 4.x and 5.x kernels — such as those shipped with RHEL 8 and Ubuntu 20.04 — run MinIO AIStor and remain supported, but modern workloads and high-performance NVMe drives demand newer kernels to operate at peak efficiency. A 6.8+ kernel unlocks critical performance features; where possible, bring older hosts to a 6.8+ kernel (for example, through a vendor hardware-enablement kernel) before production use. Older kernels bottleneck modern hardware Pairing a 4.x or 5.x kernel with current-generation hardware measurably degrades performance. Older kernels lack the storage and network stack improvements needed to drive the latest devices at their rated throughput — for example, the newest PCIe Gen5 NVMe drives and 400GbE network adapters. On such hardware, an older kernel becomes the bottleneck: MinIO AIStor cannot reach peak IOPS or line-rate network throughput until the host runs a 6.8+ kernel.
